content:
On 9 August this year, the Observatory recorded the highest temperature in its history since records began in 1884 — 36.9°C, and in Sheung Shui, the mercury climbed past 39.8°C in the early afternoon. During the sweltering heat, I hid inside this long, narrow apartment, leaving just a sliver of opening in the window for air. In such extreme heat, hot air really does pour inside, so the balcony door and the windows in the living room were all shut tight. I live on a mid-floor unit tucked between two small hills — apart from midday, the sun never reaches me from any direction. So even without air-conditioning, three ceiling fans whirring gently send down a breeze, and in a Hong Kong-style heatwave, one must learn to be grateful.

In this record-breaking heat, I stayed home to do the laundry. Just past one in the afternoon, I washed two large bedsheets with duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a heap of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the sheets and duvet covers over to dry on the other side. By half past six in the evening, I was carrying bundles of warm clothes — the kind that feel as if they have just come out of the industrial washing machines at a laundry shop — and laying them on the bed. It felt as though I had not, in half a century, enjoyed bedding this fresh from the sun. I should have been worrying about friends out in that fierce sun; the only way I could ward off the dreadfulness of the great sun was to wash each and every piece of clothing myself, one by one.

August has become a recurring nightmare. I do not know how many more times it will take to break free from the repeated goodbyes of summer. In a dream one night, I was strutting proudly, walking arm in arm with my mother, saying as we went: "My boy." I was delighted, holding tightly onto her. Then I saw, up ahead, a mysterious woman draped in a long, deep-claret cloak. My instinct was not to look at her face, but in the dream, the camera kept pulling closer, and she was a strange woman I did not recognise. When I woke, that feeling of triumph and oblivion surged up, and what stayed with me was simply: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of 10 August 2020, our family sang hymns, kissed mother's forehead, and said our goodbyes — that was a full stop. But learning to let go is a lesson one never masters in a lifetime. The unwillingness to part is a quiet wound. Six years on, regrets still surface in countless tiny details, and in my mind I replay again and again the days that led to that day, six years ago.

The regrets of parting — they come sooner or later, regardless of age, and at any stage of life. A student in my writing class wrote about her late maternal grandmother. It was a piece of reminiscence, mourning and regret. When she was very small, she had resented living with her grandmother out in the countryside. By day, with the boundless energy of a little imp, she would bicker with her grandmother; her grandmother would tweak her ear, and she would swing back, determined to give the old woman a taste of the very pain she felt. Then, peeking through the crack of the door, the little girl would catch a glimpse of her frail grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever, and walked blankly up to her grandmother and said: "I feel unwell."

Feeling unwell — that's just discomfort, just a child's way of describing pain. She was burning up with high fever, and her grandmother, without a word, dug out a clean change of clothes, dressed her on the spot, and carried her straight to the hospital to wait and see a doctor. That medicinal oil scent she used to find so disagreeable carried her, hazily, all the way to the hospital. A little while later, for some reason, the scent of the oil faded, and the little girl found herself sitting alone near the reception counter. Some grown-ups then came over and asked: "Where are your family?" Little by little, as she tried to explain, she began to cry — until the smell of medicinal oil drifted close again, and only then could she sit calmly and properly, waiting for the doctor to give her an injection and some medicine.

Back at home, the medicinal oil scent lingered as always — yet somehow it had lost its pungency. From the kitchen came the rhythmic chopping on a cutting board, and from the hot pot the fragrance of rice porridge drifting through the air. The essence of being alive needs no elaborate explanation — it is just this, simple and plain.

I wonder: when one is ill today, who is it that actually cooks the porridge?

When I was little, it was usually my father, sometimes my mother, who had the patience to "chop beef by hand" and cook porridge for me. This was the sick-day menu — and only I ever got to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would place my order in advance: "I want a beef and spring-onion porridge." It was the privilege of being unwell. Now, no one will ever cook this particular porridge for me again, and even when I'm ill, I will never taste this beef porridge again.

"If you're sick nowadays, just order FoodPanda," a friend said. Other friends will cook plain porridge or fish congee for their wives. "Sometimes I cook minced-pork porridge too." "You chop it by hand — not in a blender." "A few minutes and it's done." Such is the dignity a single pot of porridge can confer upon a person.

"In a whole lifetime, there are not many people who will cook porridge for you when you fall ill. Once you grow up, the most likely scenario is that you're the one cooking it for someone else. Most people have been through something like this. Whatever you may be feeling, say a proper goodbye, speak from the heart — whoever reads it will find some comfort for you too." I said this to the student. She looked at me, and a glint of light flickered in her eyes.

A piece of writing about a grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother… these are the stories we know, almost instinctively, how to tell.

The girl's gift was not simply her prose. She had seized upon the medicinal oil as her anchor, and circling that anchor, she gave voice to the truest of feelings between her and her closest kin. She may not have been the one who loved her grandmother most, but that time together, arranged by fate, meant that today she can never forget all her grandmother had done for her — nor can she fail to understand that human beings grow up precisely through such unknowing processes. In the end, she handed in a piece that was deeply moving, a piece that made one feel "unwell" all over again.

From being detested, trusted, then shameful, the medicinal oil had become an object of remembrance. It turned out that on the first day of primary school, the girl had been laughed at by her classmates for smelling of medicinal oil — they had called her a country bumpkin. She ran home in tears and, in a fierce voice, ordered her grandmother to scrub every single piece of clothing, front to back, with a heavy hand and loads of washing powder. Her grandmother, holding the laundry in her arms, wept. Her grandmother had been raising her since she was eight months old, and once the granddaughter grew a little older, went to school, and was exposed to the wider world, she became almost a different person — one who hurt her grandmother's heart. After she went back to live with her mother, the day came when her grandmother had developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The girl went with her mother to visit, and found that she was no longer "recognised".

"You can't be my granddaughter — she never likes talking to me," the grandmother said to the girl.

Life — at once so real, so cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my own mother? I don't think so. Or have I? I'm no more aware of it than that girl was. Family members sometimes wound one another. What matters is whether, later on, we come to understand love a little better.
